clue.text: Go-between introducing groom initially to wife-to-be

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
to introduce something is to bring it in, so one piece is put inside another

blocks.note: a woman about to be married
first letter of groom

explanation.surface: A matchmaker presents the groom to the woman he is about to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: G is slipped into BRIDE just before its last letter, giving BRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge links two separate places, so figuratively it is something that connects or mediates between two sides.

clue.text: Endure guy endlessly coming up to grab husband in big embrace

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter of the word is dropped
in a down clue, coming up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to bear is to endure or put up with
guy without its last letter
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with a man who comes along and seizes their husband in a huge hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To grab' here just means adding the husband on the end; the reversal then turns that whole group, not only the shortened guy. Read 'coming up' as upwards in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear hug is a very tight, enveloping clasp with both arms, named after the way a bear grips.

clue.text: Drive old Hillman and Tesla alternately

indicators.note: 'alternately' means every other one, so only letters at evenly spaced positions are kept

blocks.note: the Hillman Imp was a small British car made in the 1960s and 70s
second and fourth letters of Tesla

explanation.surface: Someone takes turns driving a vintage British car and a modern electric one.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hillman Imp is a defunct British small car, hence 'old'. 'Drive' looks like a motoring verb in the surface but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to push or force forward, the same as driving someone or something onward.

clue.text: £1.05 gets good girl a pet

blocks.note: a guinea was an old British coin worth 21 shillings, which is £1.05 in decimal money
PI, short for pious, is a crossword stand-in for good
G is a standard abbreviation for girl

explanation.surface: For a small sum a well-behaved child is rewarded with a pet.
explanation.walkthrough: A guinea was 21 shillings, and with 20 shillings to the pound that is £1.05. 'Good girl' looks like one phrase but is two separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinea pigs are small furry rodents commonly kept by children as household animals.

clue.text: Most of team's embarrassed for yielding

indicators.note: most but not all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a squad is a team; most of it drops the D
shy means bashful or easily embarrassed

explanation.surface: Most of the players are red-faced at giving in to the opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yielding' reads as giving way in the surface; here it is the adjective meaning soft to the touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something squashy gives under pressure, which is the physical sense of yielding: soft and compressible.

clue.text: Record time making garment

blocks.note: a single is a record with one main track
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone sets a record time while sewing clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record time' looks like a fixed phrase for speed, but the words split into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn as an undershirt or by athletes, so it is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Ruffled the in-crowd?

blocks.note: first meaning: disturbed or agitated
second meaning, read as two words: a set that is up, i.e. in fashion

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: UP means fashionable or in, and a SET is a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Being upset means being bothered or flustered, just as feathers that are ruffled signal agitation.

clue.text: Fare dodgers pull off hiding in ship

indicators.note: something hiding in a place is concealed inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: SS stands for steamship
to tow away is to pull a vehicle off

explanation.surface: Passengers avoiding paying get dragged out from their hiding place aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull off' suggests succeeding at something, but here it is a phrasal tow, as of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowaways travel hidden on a vessel without buying a ticket, which makes them evaders of the fare.

clue.text: Great in the old days: you lit pipe inside

indicators.note: 'lit' is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger into a new order
one piece goes inside the other, so it is enclosed

blocks.note: ye is the old form of you, as the link phrase flags
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone reminisces that long ago it was wonderful to light a pipe indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lit' looks like the past tense of light; here it means drunk. 'In the old days' tells you to use the archaic YE.
explanation.definitionFit: Yippee is an exclamation of delight, used just as one might shout 'Great!' on hearing good news.

clue.text: Limited sex during punishment

indicators.note: something happening during another event falls within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a fine is a monetary penalty
IT is a crossword euphemism for sex, or sex appeal

explanation.surface: Restrictions on intercourse are imposed as part of someone's sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex or sex appeal comes from old phrases like Clara Bow being the 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Finite describes something having bounds or an end, the same as limited in extent or quantity.

clue.text: For example, a frog in Namibia mutated, acquiring pinkish extremities

indicators.note: a mutation changes form, so the letters change their order
extremities are the far ends, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: taken as written for the rearrangement
first and last letters of pinkish

explanation.surface: A frog in southern Africa has evolved, growing pink-tipped limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremities' suggests limbs like toes, but it means the end letters of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Frogs belong to the animal class that lives both in water and on land, so a frog is an instance of it.

clue.text: Political party's infiltrated by 'double 0' spy

indicators.note: an infiltrated group has an outsider slipped inside, so one piece gets placed within another

blocks.note: the Scottish National Party
two letter Os, which look like zeros

explanation.surface: A party has been penetrated by a James Bond style secret agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double 0' evokes 007, but here the zeros are simply two letter Os. The SNP is the Scottish National Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A snoop is someone who pries into others' affairs, so the noun is a close match for a spy.

clue.text: Own clothing line is cut by 50%

indicators.note: clothing wraps around a body, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: to own something is to have it
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A designer's own fashion range is being marked down by half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Own clothing line' reads as a fashion brand, but 'clothing' is a verb meaning wrapping round.
explanation.definitionFit: To halve something is to reduce it to half, which is exactly reducing it by fifty per cent.

clue.text: Unable to relax, has some vanilla tea served

indicators.note: having some of something means taking just a part, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of vanilla, all of tea and the start of served

explanation.surface: A tense person is given a cup of vanilla-flavoured tea to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across three words of the clue, starting inside 'vanilla' and finishing early in 'served'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ill at ease is an idiom for feeling uncomfortable or anxious, the state of someone who cannot settle.

clue.text: Struggle repeatedly parking large convertible

indicators.note: something convertible can be changed into another form, so these letters can be rearranged

blocks.note: P for parking, twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A driver keeps failing to park a big open-topped car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convertible' looks like a car in the surface but is the signal to rearrange. P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking.
explanation.definitionFit: To grapple is to wrestle or fight with something, whether a physical opponent or a difficult problem.

clue.text: Say 'Sorry I go so pale at sea'

indicators.note: being at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A seasick passenger excuses themselves for turning white on a voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the seasick picture literally, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To apologise is to express regret, and uttering the word sorry is the basic way of doing that.

clue.text: Classy headgear's better at accommodating head of hair

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
accommodating something means giving it room inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: to top is to better or outdo
taken as written
first letter of hair

explanation.surface: Smart hats are good at fitting over your head of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes into the combined TOPAT, landing between the two words to make TOP HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A top hat is a tall silk hat worn with formal dress, so it is an elegant item worn on the head.

clue.text: Judge engaged in pure finesse to cut bigotry

indicators.note: to finesse is to manoeuvre deftly, so the letters are skilfully moved around
something engaged in an activity is caught up inside it, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
to dice is to cut into small cubes
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A judge sets out with real skill to stamp out intolerance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finesse' reads as a noun meaning delicacy, but it works as a verb, telling you to manoeuvre letters; the judge then lands inside the result rather than at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Prejudice is a preconceived hostile opinion about a group, which is what bigotry consists of.

clue.text: Fail to recall counterfeit model

blocks.note: to forge is to counterfeit
the Model T was Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: Someone can't remember which fake design they made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counterfeit model' looks like a fake item, but it splits into a verb and the Ford Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: To forget is to be unable to bring something back to mind, which is the same as not remembering it.

clue.text: Tutor taking hour off with first kid in A&E gets something nice to eat

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so a letter is dropped from the word
first means the opening letter, so only the start of the word is kept
one piece is put in the other, so it is enclosed

blocks.note: to tutor is to teach
H is the abbreviation for hour; this letter is the one taken off
taken as written
first letter of kid

explanation.surface: A teacher on a break takes the first child to hospital and gets a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tutor' looks like a noun but is the verb teach; H is the abbreviation for hour. A&E is the British name for a hospital emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a light, sweet bun with dried fruit, usually toasted and buttered, which is a pleasant treat.

clue.text: Note Spurs playing without Kane finally look smarter

indicators.note: playing around with letters puts them into a new order
finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept
in its old sense without means outside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: D is a note in the musical scale
taken as written, then rearranged
last letter of Kane

explanation.surface: A comment that Tottenham play better without their star striker Harry Kane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' seems to mean lacking, which would remove letters, but it means outside: rearranged SPURS goes around E. Spurs is Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress up is a phrasal verb for putting on smart or formal clothes, improving your appearance.

clue.text: Thought of French journalist capturing space in print

indicators.note: capturing something means holding it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: de is French for of
an em is a printer's unit of space
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A French reporter's opinion is written down with a gap left in the copy.
explanation.walkthrough: DE plus ED makes DEED, which captures EM in its middle. 'Thought' is a past participle here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Deemed means judged or considered, as in 'it was deemed unwise', the same as thought in that sense.

clue.text: Sick postie keeping uniform is poignant

indicators.note: something sick is in poor order, so its letters are disordered
to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An ill postman still wearing their work clothes is a moving sight.
explanation.walkthrough: A postie is British slang for a postman. 'Uniform' looks like the postal outfit but is the code word for U.
explanation.definitionFit: Piteous describes something that arouses pity, so a sight that touches the emotions deeply fits it.

clue.text: Stopped heartless revolutionary dictator

indicators.note: without a heart the middle is missing, so the central letter is removed
a revolution overturns the existing order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Stopped loses one of its two middle Ps

explanation.surface: A cruel rebel tyrant has been halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' sounds like the dictator's politics, but it tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a ruler with absolute power, usually used cruelly, which is what a dictator is.

clue.text: Discharge is horribly near to blocking Devon river

indicators.note: something done horribly is badly mangled, so the letters are mixed up
a blockage sits inside a channel, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the Exe is a river flowing through Exeter in the English county of Devon
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Pollution is being released alarmingly close to a river in south-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharge' looks like effluent in the surface, but it is the legal sense of releasing someone from blame.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate is to clear someone of blame or obligation, the formal sense in which a court discharges a defendant.

clue.text: Vote for point supported by half of speeches

indicators.note: in a down clue what is supported sits on top, so the order is fixed top to bottom
taking half leaves only part, so the rest of the word is dropped

blocks.note: E is a compass point, east
lectures are speeches; the first four of its eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone backs a proposal endorsed in half the addresses given.
explanation.walkthrough: Lectures, eight letters, halves to LECT. In a down clue 'supported by' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to choose someone by ballot, which is what casting a vote for a candidate does.

clue.text: Fellow captured by detachment is in bad shape

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: a detachment of troops is a military unit
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A man taken prisoner by a squad of soldiers is in poor condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detachment' suggests aloofness, but it is a body of troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfit describes a body lacking physical fitness, so someone out of condition is in poor physical shape.

clue.text: Both sides in final broadcast show panache

indicators.note: both sides are the two edges, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of final
to air is to broadcast

explanation.surface: Both teams in a televised cup final play with style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a TV programme next to 'broadcast', but it just joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair means stylish originality or natural talent, which is close to panache, a confident stylish manner.

clue.text: Articulated lever for jackpot

indicators.note: to articulate is to pronounce words, so it is the sound that counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: to prise is to lever something open

explanation.surface: A hinged lever on a slot machine pays out the big win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulated' looks like jointed, as of a lorry or lever, but it means spoken. PRISE is the British spelling of prying open.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackpot is the top award in a game or lottery, so it is a kind of reward won by chance.

clue.text: Am with old Queen and I may ring for coffee

blocks.note: taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, was the late Queen's royal cipher
taken as written
may and can both express permission
O is round like a ring

explanation.surface: Someone at court asks whether they may call for a hot drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call, but it is the ring-shaped letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: An americano is an espresso diluted with hot water, a standard order in coffee shops.

clue.text: The Stage has article on hosting panto regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept
a host has guests inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the definite article
RE means on, in the sense of concerning
second and fourth letters of panto

explanation.surface: The trade newspaper The Stage runs a piece about a pantomime production.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stage is a British newspaper for the performing arts, but here it means drama in general. A panto is a British family Christmas show.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre and the stage are both used as umbrella terms for the acting profession and dramatic performance.

clue.text: Waste when teacher with education degree retired

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir
BEd is a Bachelor of Education

explanation.surface: A qualified teacher's skills go to waste once they stop working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' looks like stopping work in the surface, but it signals going backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered rubbish or wreckage, so it is a synonym for waste material.
